content.content:
## Switching Between Languages

Have you ever started a sentence in Norwegian and finished it in English, or dropped an English word into a Norwegian conversation because it just *fit* better? If so, you have practised code-switching -- and far from being a sign of confusion or laziness, it is a sophisticated communicative strategy used by multilingual speakers all over the world.

**Code-switching** is the practice of alternating between two or more languages within a single conversation, sentence, or even phrase. It comes in three main types. **Inter-sentential switching** happens at sentence boundaries: "Det var en veldig god film. I really loved the ending." **Intra-sentential switching** happens within a single sentence: "Kan du sende meg den file-en?" And **tag-switching** inserts a tag or filler from one language into another: "Det blir bra, you know?" Crucially, code-switching requires high competence in *both* languages -- you must know the grammar of each well enough to combine them without creating confusion.

## Why We Code-Switch

Linguists have identified several social functions of code-switching, and recognising them reveals just how purposeful the practice is.

First is **solidarity and group identity**: switching to a shared minority language signals in-group membership -- Norwegian-Pakistani teenagers might switch to Urdu to mark solidarity. Second is **emphasis and expressiveness**: a switch can add emotional force, as in "That was ikke greit!" Third is **topic-related switching**: a Norwegian student might switch to English when discussing technology, gaming, or social media, because those domains feel more natural in English. Fourth is **quotation and reported speech**: speakers often switch when quoting someone -- "Og da sa han, 'no way, that's impossible!'" Fifth is **exclusion or inclusion**: speaking a language not everyone understands can create or dissolve boundaries. Sixth is **accommodation**: switching to the language of the person you are talking to, out of politeness. And seventh is **identity performance**: code-switching can signal a cosmopolitan, bilingual, multicultural identity.

Consider a real example -- two Norwegian university students: "Har du lest den artikkelen til i morgen?" / "Ja, men den var so confusing. Hele den delen om methodology var basically impossible." / "Same. Jeg tror vi burde fikse en study group." Here we see intra-sentential switching ("den var so confusing"), topic-related switching ("methodology"), tag-switching ("Same."), and English terms integrated into Norwegian grammar ("study group," "gruppechatten"). This conversation is completely natural for young Norwegians. The switching follows predictable patterns and serves clear functions -- it is not miscommunication but skilled use of multilingual resources.

options.text: As a sign of weak language skills
As skilled use of multilingual resources, following predictable patterns

## Translanguaging: One Mind, One Repertoire

Code-switching assumes that speakers move *between* separate language systems. But a newer concept, **translanguaging**, offers a different picture. It suggests that multilingual speakers do not have separate language boxes in their minds at all -- instead, they draw flexibly from a single, integrated **linguistic repertoire**.

The contrast is illuminating. Code-switching views languages as *separate systems* and focuses on the switch itself; it is sometimes seen as "mixing" and has traditionally been discouraged in schools. Translanguaging views languages as *one integrated repertoire* and focuses on the speaker's full resources; it is seen as natural and strategic, and is increasingly encouraged in education.

That shift toward education is significant. Traditionally, schools operated on a "one language at a time" principle -- Norwegian in Norwegian class, English in English class -- and expected students to keep their languages strictly separate. Translanguaging challenges this. Its benefits in the classroom are real: students can use their full linguistic repertoire to make meaning, it validates their multilingual identities, it deepens understanding by allowing comparison between languages, it helps students with weaker target-language skills participate more fully, and it reflects how language actually works in multilingual communities. In practice, a student writing an English essay might brainstorm ideas in Norwegian first, look up key concepts in both languages, and discuss the topic in whichever language helps them think most clearly -- before producing the final text in English. It is also worth distinguishing **borrowing** (incorporating a word from one language into another, often adapted -- like Norwegian "å surfe" from English "to surf") from full code-switching: borrowing involves single integrated words, while switching alternates between language systems.

questions.task: How does translanguaging view a multilingual speaker's languages?

options.text: As one integrated linguistic repertoire rather than separate systems
As a single language with no variation
As always in conflict with each other

questions.solution: Translanguaging sees languages as one integrated repertoire that the speaker draws from flexibly, in contrast to code-switching, which assumes movement between separate systems.

questions.task: How is translanguaging increasingly viewed in education?

options.text: As something to be strictly forbidden
As natural and strategic, and increasingly encouraged
As proof of poor language skills

questions.solution: Translanguaging is increasingly encouraged in classrooms because it validates students' multilingual identities and can deepen learning, challenging the old 'one language at a time' rule.

questions.task: What is 'borrowing', as distinct from code-switching?

options.text: Refusing to use any foreign words
Incorporating a single word from one language into another, often adapted (e.g. 'å surfe')

questions.solution: Borrowing involves taking a single word into another language, often with grammatical adaptation (Norwegian 'å surfe' from 'to surf'). Code-switching alternates between language systems.

questions.task: Which is a benefit of translanguaging in the classroom?

options.text: It forces students to forget their first language
It bans the use of Norwegian entirely
It validates students' multilingual identities and lets them use their full resources

questions.solution: Translanguaging lets students use their full linguistic repertoire to make meaning, validates their identities, and helps weaker students participate -- reflecting how multilingual communication really works.
